title: The joint stock company: separate person, board and types
summary: What a joint stock company is, how the board and independent directors manage it, how companies are classified, and the one person company.

chunks.heading: A company is an artificial person
chunks.explanation_md:
A **joint stock company** evolved as a voluntary association of persons who contribute capital as **members or shareholders**. All undertakings incorporated and registered under the **Companies Act** are called companies.

The key idea: a company is an **artificial person created by law**, with a **separate legal entity**, **perpetual succession** and a **common seal**. The slide quotes a Chief Justice's description of a corporation as an artificial being, invisible and intangible, existing only in the eyes of the law.

Because of this, the life of the company does **not depend on the life of its members**. It is created by process of law and can be ended only by a process established by law. Compare this with the sole proprietor and the partnership, which end on death.

key_terms.meaning: An artificial person created by law, with a separate legal entity, perpetual succession and common seal.
The company's life does not depend on the life of its members; it ends only by a legal process.

chunks.exam_line: Company = artificial person, separate legal entity, perpetual succession, common seal; not affected by members' death.

chunks.heading: Board of directors and independent directors
chunks.explanation_md:
Not all shareholders take part in running the business, so they elect representatives called the **Board of Directors**. The board is responsible for managing the organization and exercising its rights and responsibilities, by **hiring the senior management**.

- **Publication of financial results**: a joint stock company must file its **annual report with the registrar of companies** at the end of the year.
- **Independent directors**: the government has made it mandatory to have independent directors, with authority and matching accountability. Every listed public company must have **at least one-third** of its board as independent directors. Under SEBI LODR regulations, if the regular Chairperson is an executive director or related to the promoters, it is at least **half (50%)**.
- **Independent non-executive directors** are outsiders with judgment and logic who can bring fresh ideas and act as a **watchdog** protecting stakeholders (shareholders, suppliers and customers) from an overzealous management.

key_terms.meaning: Representatives elected by shareholders to manage the company, including by hiring senior management.
Outsiders who bring fresh ideas and act as a watchdog for stakeholders.

chunks.heading: Classifying joint stock companies
chunks.explanation_md:
The slide sorts companies in three ways.

- **On the basis of incorporation**: chartered companies, statutory companies, registered companies.
- **According to liability**: companies limited by shares, companies limited by guarantee.
- **According to transferability of shares**: private limited company, public limited company, and one person company.

Expect to be asked for these three bases and their types.

key_terms.meaning: Incorporation (chartered, statutory, registered); liability (by shares, by guarantee); transferability of shares (private, public, one person).

chunks.exam_line: Three bases: incorporation, liability, transferability of shares.

chunks.heading: One person company
chunks.explanation_md:
The slide is a picture of a man in a suit with six labelled arrows about the **One Person Company (OPC)**, compared with a private limited company:

- **Cost to register**: almost the same as a private limited company, a bit lower.
- **Persons required**: two, same as a private limited company.
- **Shareholding**: one is enough in an OPC; two in a private limited company.
- **NRIs or FDI**: NRIs or foreign nationals cannot participate in an OPC.
- **Limitations**: an OPC must be mandatorily converted into a private limited company once certain conditions are met.
- **Post incorporation**: an OPC may have difficulties obtaining other licences or registrations.

key_terms.meaning: A company where one shareholder is enough; it must be converted into a private limited company once certain conditions are met, and NRIs or foreign nationals cannot participate.

chunks.exam_line: OPC: one shareholder is enough, no NRIs or foreign nationals, must convert to a private limited company once conditions are met.

questions.stem: Explain why a joint stock company is called an artificial person.
questions.model_answer_md:
A **joint stock company** is an **artificial person created by law**.

- It has a **separate legal entity** from its members.
- It has **perpetual succession**: its life does not depend on the life of its members.
- It has a **common seal**.
- It is created by a legal process and can end only by a process established by law.

A sole proprietorship or partnership, by contrast, is dissolved on a death.

questions.stem: Explain the role of independent non-executive directors.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Independent non-executive directors** are outsiders on the board.

- The government made it mandatory to have them, with authority and matching accountability, so the board is empowered and effective.
- A listed public company needs at least one-third of its board independent; at least half if the Chairperson is an executive director or related to the promoters.
- They bring judgment, logic and fresh ideas and act as a **watchdog** for stakeholders (shareholders, suppliers and customers) against an overzealous management.

questions.stem: Differentiate a One Person Company from a private limited company using the points in the deck.
questions.model_answer_md:
Both are companies with a similar registration cost, but they differ on a few points.

- **Shareholding**: one is enough in an OPC; two in a private limited company.
- **Foreign participation**: NRIs or foreign nationals cannot participate in an OPC.
- **Limitations**: an OPC must be converted into a private limited company once certain conditions are met.
- **After incorporation**: an OPC may find it hard to obtain other licences or registrations.
- **Cost**: almost the same as private limited, a bit lower.

questions.stem: Explain the joint stock company as a form of business: its nature, how it is managed, and how companies are classified.
questions.model_answer_md:
A **joint stock company** is a voluntary association of persons who contribute capital as members or shareholders. Undertakings incorporated and registered under the Companies Act are called companies.

**Nature.** A company is an **artificial person created by law**, with a **separate legal entity**, **perpetual succession** and a **common seal**. Its life does not depend on its members and it can be ended only by a legal process.

**Management.** Since not all shareholders take part, they elect a **Board of Directors**, which manages the company and exercises its rights and responsibilities by hiring senior management. The company must file its annual report with the registrar of companies each year. **Independent directors**, with authority and accountability, are mandatory: at least one-third of a listed public company board, and at least half where the Chairperson is an executive director or related to the promoters. They act as a watchdog for stakeholders.

**Classification.**
- On incorporation: chartered, statutory and registered companies.
- On liability: limited by shares, limited by guarantee.
- On transferability of shares: private limited, public limited and one person company.

**One person company.** One shareholder is enough, NRIs cannot take part, and it must convert to a private limited company once conditions are met.

In conclusion, a company's separate identity and board-led management separate it from the simpler forms.
